title: Somatic and Visceral Motor and Sensory Pathways
subject: Nervous System (NEUR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter follows motor commands out of the central nervous system and visceral sensory signals back in. It traces the lateral corticospinal tract from cortex to the anterior horn, explains why upper and lower motor neuron lesions look so different, contrasts the one-neuron somatic and two-neuron autonomic motor pathways, and shows how visceral pain and baroreceptor signals reach the cord and medulla. Board questions usually describe a patient and ask you to place the lesion. If you know where each tract runs, where it crosses, and which artery supplies it, you can predict the findings of motor neuron disease and the classic spinal cord syndromes from first principles.
prerequisites: Neuron structure, synaptic transmission, and fiber classes (A alpha, A delta, B, C)
Cross-sectional anatomy of the spinal cord: gray horns, white funiculi, dorsal and ventral roots
The stretch reflex: muscle spindle, Ia afferent, and alpha motor neuron

connections.how: Spinal cord syndromes combine motor loss from this chapter with the dorsal column and spinothalamic losses taught there.
The arteries supplying motor cortex, internal capsule, brainstem, and anterior cord decide which corticospinal segment an infarct removes.
The baroreceptor reflex links CN IX and CN X afferents and the nucleus solitarius to moment-to-moment control of heart rate and vascular tone.
Vitamin B12 is a cofactor for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, so its deficiency causes both megaloblastic anemia and myelin failure in the cord.
Poliovirus, Treponema pallidum, and SMN1 loss each damage a specific neuronal population, which explains their distinct patterns of weakness and sensory loss.

A stretch receptor in the wall of the carotid sinus or aortic arch that signals arterial pressure.

sections.title: The lateral corticospinal tract from cortex to anterior horn

blocks.text: The lateral corticospinal tract carries voluntary, skilled movement, especially of the distal limbs. Its neurons are upper motor neurons (UMNs): their cell bodies lie in cerebral cortex and their axons descend without interruption to the spinal cord. About one third of the fibers arise in primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus, Brodmann area 4), about one third in premotor and supplementary motor cortex (area 6), and the rest in parietal somatosensory cortex. Giant pyramidal (Betz) cells in layer V of area 4 supply only about 3% of the fibers, but they are the largest and fastest.

The precentral gyrus is mapped by body part. The leg and foot lie on the medial surface in the paracentral lobule, supplied by the anterior cerebral artery, while the trunk, arm, hand, and face lie on the lateral convexity, supplied by the middle cerebral artery. This is why an anterior cerebral artery infarct weakens mainly the opposite leg and a middle cerebral artery infarct weakens mainly the opposite face and arm.

Middle part of the cerebral peduncle (crus cerebri)

blocks.caption: Above the decussation the tract serves the opposite side of the body; below it, the tract serves the same side.

blocks.text: In the internal capsule the corticospinal fibers for arm and leg are packed into the posterior limb, with corticobulbar fibers for the face near the genu. This compact bundle is supplied by lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery and by the anterior choroidal artery, so a small lacunar infarct can produce dense pure motor hemiparesis of the opposite face, arm, and leg. In the pons the tract is broken up by pontine nuclei, and it regroups on the ventral medulla as the pyramid.

At the cervicomedullary junction most fibers cross and descend in the lateral funiculus. The uncrossed remainder (about 10%) forms the anterior corticospinal tract, and most of those fibers cross at their own segment in the anterior white commissure to reach motor neurons for axial and proximal muscles. Lateral tract axons end mainly on interneurons, but some synapse directly on alpha motor neurons in the lateral anterior horn, the cells that drive the fine finger movements this tract is best known for. The alpha motor neuron is the lower motor neuron (LMN) and the final common pathway: its axon leaves in the ventral root and spinal nerve to the motor end plate.

sections.title: Upper versus lower motor neuron lesions, ALS, poliomyelitis, and SMA

blocks.text: Resting muscle tone is the background activity of the stretch reflex: spindle Ia afferents excite alpha motor neurons, and descending pathways set how excitable that loop is. Upper motor neuron lesions and lower motor neuron lesions disturb this loop in opposite ways, which is why their signs are near mirror images.

A UMN lesion removes descending control while the reflex arc stays intact. The lesion usually damages corticospinal fibers together with the cortical fibers that drive inhibitory reticulospinal output, leaving facilitatory vestibulospinal and reticulospinal influences unopposed. Alpha and gamma motor neurons become hyperexcitable, so stretch reflexes are exaggerated: tone rises in a velocity-dependent way (spasticity, often with a clasp-knife quality), reflexes are brisk, and clonus may appear. Loss of corticospinal input also releases the Babinski sign, an extensor plantar response that is normal in infants before the tract is fully myelinated. Atrophy is mild, from disuse. An acute UMN lesion is often flaccid and areflexic for days before spasticity develops. A lesion confined to the corticospinal tract, as in a pure pyramidal lesion, gives weakness and a Babinski sign with little spasticity, because the reticulospinal fibers are spared.

An LMN lesion (anterior horn cell, ventral root, or peripheral nerve) cuts the efferent limb of the reflex arc, so the muscle is weak, flaccid, and hyporeflexic or areflexic. Denervated muscle loses neural activity and trophic support and wastes markedly within weeks. Irritable motor neurons and axons fire spontaneously, and each discharge of a whole motor unit shows as a fasciculation.

Groups of muscles, one side or below a level
Muscles of the affected segment, root, or nerve
blocks.caption: Both columns describe weakness; the other signs locate the lesion above or at the anterior horn.

blocks.text: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) destroys both populations: Betz cells and corticospinal axons (scarring the lateral columns) and anterior horn and brainstem motor neurons (causing amyotrophy, muscle wasting). The result is a mixture of UMN and LMN signs, often in the same limb, such as a wasted, fasciculating arm with brisk reflexes and a Babinski sign. Sensory neurons are spared, and so, usually, are the oculomotor nuclei and the sacral motor neurons controlling the sphincters. Most cases are sporadic; about 10% are familial, with C9orf72 and SOD1 mutations among the known causes.

Poliomyelitis and spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) damage only anterior horn cells, so they give pure LMN signs with intact sensation. Poliovirus, an enterovirus spread by the fecal-oral route, replicates in pharyngeal and intestinal lymphoid tissue, reaches the bloodstream, and in a small minority of infections destroys anterior horn cells, causing asymmetric flaccid paralysis. SMA is autosomal recessive loss of the SMN1 gene on chromosome 5q. Its protein is needed to assemble small nuclear ribonucleoproteins for splicing, and motor neurons degenerate without it; the number of copies of the similar SMN2 gene modifies severity. The severe infantile form presents as a floppy infant with tongue fasciculations and absent reflexes.

blocks.predict: A small infarct destroys only the medullary pyramid on one side. Will the opposite limbs be strongly spastic?
blocks.explain: Spasticity depends mainly on loss of the cortical drive to inhibitory reticulospinal pathways, which do not run in the pyramid. A pure pyramidal lesion causes weakness, loss of fine finger movement, and a Babinski sign, but only mild changes in tone.

blocks.text: Somatic motor output uses one neuron. The alpha motor neuron in the anterior horn, or in a cranial nerve motor nucleus, sends a large myelinated axon straight to skeletal muscle. At the neuromuscular junction acetylcholine (ACh) binds muscle-type nicotinic receptors (NM), ligand-gated cation channels that depolarize the end plate. Skeletal muscle has no intrinsic activity, so this input is always excitatory: without it the muscle is paralyzed.

Visceral (autonomic) motor output uses two neurons. A preganglionic neuron in the CNS sends a thinly myelinated B fiber to an autonomic ganglion, where it releases ACh onto neuronal nicotinic receptors (NN). The postganglionic neuron sends an unmyelinated C fiber to smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, or glands. Instead of a specialized end plate, it releases transmitter from varicosities along its terminal branches, so the signal spreads to many cells. Visceral targets already have their own tone, rhythm, or secretion, so autonomic input modulates them, and the receptor on the target decides whether the effect is excitatory or inhibitory.

steps: Preganglionic cell in the intermediolateral column (T1 to L2)

blocks.caption: White rami exist only from T1 to L2, while gray rami join every spinal nerve, so sympathetic fibers reach the whole body wall.

blocks.text: The adrenal medulla is the main exception to the two-neuron rule. Preganglionic sympathetic fibers in the splanchnic nerves end directly on chromaffin cells, which come from neural crest like postganglionic neurons and release mostly epinephrine into the blood as a hormone.

Because the NM and NN receptors have different subunits, disease and drugs can separate the two systems. Myasthenia gravis antibodies target the muscle nicotinic receptor, so weakness occurs without autonomic symptoms, while a ganglionic nicotinic blocker such as hexamethonium interrupts both sympathetic and parasympathetic output and leaves skeletal muscle untouched. Lambert-Eaton syndrome targets presynaptic P/Q-type Ca2+ channels used at both kinds of terminal, so it causes both weakness and autonomic signs such as dry mouth.

blocks.predict: Would a toxin that blocks ACh release from all cholinergic terminals affect only skeletal muscle?
blocks.explain: No. Every somatic motor terminal, every preganglionic terminal, and every parasympathetic postganglionic terminal releases ACh, so the toxin would cause skeletal paralysis together with loss of autonomic ganglionic transmission and parasympathetic effects, such as dry mouth, dilated pupils, and urinary retention.

blocks.text: The dorsal columns (fine touch, vibration, and position sense) ascend on the same side and cross in the medulla. The lateral corticospinal tract descends on the same side after crossing in the medulla. The spinothalamic tract (pain and temperature) crosses within one or two segments of entry and ascends on the opposite side. Blood supply divides the cord the same way: one anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two thirds, and paired posterior spinal arteries supply the dorsal columns and dorsal horns.

Subacute combined degeneration results from vitamin B12 deficiency. B12 is the cofactor for methionine synthase, which supplies S-adenosylmethionine for methylation reactions, and for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, so methylmalonic acid and homocysteine rise. Myelin of long, heavily myelinated axons fails, with vacuolar change beginning in the cervical and upper thoracic cord. Losing the dorsal columns causes symmetric paresthesias, loss of vibration and position sense, and sensory ataxia with a positive Romberg sign; losing the lateral corticospinal tracts adds spastic weakness and Babinski signs. Knee reflexes are often brisk, but ankle reflexes may be lost when a peripheral neuropathy coexists. Anemia can be absent.

Tabes dorsalis is a late form of neurosyphilis (Treponema pallidum) in which the dorsal roots, mainly lumbosacral, are inflamed and degenerate. The dorsal columns degenerate secondarily because they are the central branches of the same dorsal root ganglion neurons. Position sense and reflexes are lost together, because the afferent limb of the stretch reflex is cut, while strength and plantar responses stay normal.

Anterior spinal artery infarction removes the anterior two thirds: corticospinal tracts, spinothalamic tracts, anterior horns, and descending autonomic fibers to the bladder. Vibration and position sense survive because the posterior spinal arteries are intact. The mid-thoracic cord is a watershed, so aortic dissection, aortic surgery, or severe hypotension that compromises the great anterior radicular artery (artery of Adamkiewicz) is the classic cause.

Complete transection removes every tract at the level. At first, sudden loss of descending facilitation silences the cord below (spinal shock), giving flaccid paralysis, areflexia, and an atonic bladder; lesions above about T6 also remove sympathetic outflow, causing hypotension and bradycardia. Over days to weeks spinal reflexes recover and become exaggerated, so UMN signs appear below the level, with LMN signs and a band of sensory loss at the level itself.

blocks.title: Worked example: paraplegia after aortic repair
blocks.text: After thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm repair, a 68-year-old cannot move his legs. Pinprick and temperature are absent below the umbilicus on both sides, yet he feels a tuning fork at both ankles and knows which way his toes are moved. Step 1: both legs weak means both corticospinal tracts. Step 2: bilateral loss of pain and temperature means both spinothalamic tracts. Step 3: preserved vibration and position means intact dorsal columns, so the posterior spinal arteries were spared. Step 4: the umbilicus is the T10 dermatome, so the lesion lies at or above about T10. Only loss of the anterior spinal artery territory fits, from interrupted flow through the great anterior radicular artery during aortic clamping. His legs are flaccid and areflexic now (spinal shock), but spasticity and Babinski signs should develop.

sections.title: Visceral sensory pathways: pain and baroreceptor reflexes

blocks.text: Visceral afferents are sparse, thinly myelinated A delta and unmyelinated C fibers. Their endings respond to distension, ischemia, inflammation, and traction, but not to cutting or burning, which is why a bowel can be cut without pain while distension hurts. Two routes carry them: pain afferents travel back with sympathetic nerves, while afferents for unconscious reflexes travel with parasympathetic nerves, chiefly CN IX and CN X.

blocks.title: Route of visceral pain from a thoracic or abdominal organ
steps: Nociceptor in organ wall: distension, ischemia, inflammation
Visceral plexus and prevertebral ganglion, passing without synapse
Splanchnic nerve to the sympathetic chain
White ramus to the spinal nerve
Cell body in a T1 to L2 dorsal root ganglion
Dorsal horn neuron that also receives skin input
Spinothalamic tract to thalamus and cortex
Pain felt in that segment's dermatome
blocks.caption: Visceral pain follows sympathetic nerves backward, so its segment matches the organ's sympathetic supply.

blocks.text: Referred pain arises from convergence: visceral afferents end on dorsal horn neurons that also carry input from a dermatome, and the brain, more familiar with skin, assigns the signal to the body wall. Early visceral pain is therefore dull, poorly localized, and midline, because most gut organs are midline in origin and have bilateral innervation. In the pelvis, organs that touch the peritoneum send pain with sympathetic fibers, but organs below the pelvic pain line send it with the pelvic splanchnic nerves to S2 to S4.

blocks.title: Common referral patterns
rows: Substernal, left chest, medial left arm
C3 to C5 via phrenic nerve
blocks.caption: The diaphragm is the exception: its central pain travels in the somatic phrenic nerve, not with sympathetics.

blocks.title: Worked example: why appendicitis pain moves
blocks.text: Appendicitis often begins as vague periumbilical pain that later shifts to the right lower quadrant. Step 1: the inflamed, distended appendix stimulates visceral afferents that travel with sympathetic fibers to the T10 segment. Step 2: the T10 dorsal horn also serves the umbilical dermatome, so the pain is referred there, dull and midline. Step 3: as inflammation reaches the overlying parietal peritoneum, somatic nerves of the abdominal wall are stimulated. Step 4: somatic afferents are dense and well mapped, so the pain becomes sharp and localized over the appendix.

Baroreceptors are stretch-sensitive endings in the wall of the carotid sinus, at the origin of the internal carotid artery, and in the aortic arch. Carotid sinus fibers run in the carotid sinus nerve, a branch of CN IX, and aortic arch fibers in CN X. Both enter the medulla, run in the solitary tract, and synapse in the nucleus solitarius (nucleus of the solitary tract). Carotid receptors fire little below about 50 to 60 mmHg, respond most steeply near normal mean pressure, and saturate near 180 mmHg; they respond more to a changing pressure than to a steady one. Carotid body and aortic body chemoreceptors use the same nerves.

blocks.title: Baroreceptor reflex
steps: Arterial pressure rises; vessel walls stretch
Carotid sinus (CN IX) and aortic arch (CN X) firing increases
Nucleus solitarius is excited
Vagal output rises; medullary sympathetic drive falls
Heart rate, contractility, and vascular resistance fall
Pressure returns toward the set point
blocks.caption: The same loop runs in reverse when pressure falls, as on standing.

blocks.predict: If both carotid sinus nerves and the aortic baroreceptor fibers are cut, what happens to blood pressure?
blocks.explain: Tonic inhibition from the nucleus solitarius falls, so sympathetic drive rises and pressure increases at first. Over time the average pressure changes little, but it swings widely with posture and activity because no fast negative feedback remains. Baroreceptors buffer short-term changes; they also reset within days, so they do not set the long-term level.

integration.text: Anatomy and blood supply decide the pattern of deficit. The corticospinal tract crosses once, low in the medulla, so laterality depends on whether a lesion lies above or below the decussation, and each named artery removes a predictable segment: the lenticulostriate branches take the internal capsule, the anterior spinal artery the anterior cord. Biochemistry, microbiology, and genetics explain which cells fail: B12 deficiency attacks myelin, Treponema pallidum the dorsal roots, poliovirus and SMN1 loss the anterior horn cells, and ALS both motor neuron populations while sensory neurons survive.

Physiology links the visceral pathways to other systems. The same nucleus solitarius receives baroreceptor, chemoreceptor, and taste input, so the medulla integrates cardiovascular and respiratory reflexes, while visceral pain referral reflects embryologic segment origin rather than the organ's adult position. The rules have limits: early lesions may be flaccid before spasticity appears, overlapping neuropathy can blunt expected hyperreflexia, and dermatome and referral maps vary between individuals and sources.

summary: The lateral corticospinal tract runs precentral gyrus, posterior limb of the internal capsule, middle cerebral peduncle, basilar pons, pyramid, decussation, lateral funiculus, anterior horn.
About 85% to 90% of corticospinal fibers cross in the caudal medulla; lesions above the decussation cause contralateral weakness, cord lesions cause ipsilateral weakness.
UMN lesions release the stretch reflex: spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign, mild atrophy; LMN lesions cut it: flaccidity, areflexia, fasciculations, marked atrophy.
ALS gives mixed UMN and LMN signs with spared sensation; poliomyelitis and SMA destroy anterior horn cells and give pure LMN signs.
Somatic motor is one neuron with ACh on NM receptors and always excites; visceral motor is two neurons with ACh on NN in the ganglion and excitatory or inhibitory effects at the target.
Subacute combined degeneration takes dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts; tabes takes dorsal roots and dorsal columns with areflexia and normal strength.
Anterior spinal artery infarction spares only the dorsal columns; complete transection removes everything below the level, starting with spinal shock.
Visceral pain travels with sympathetic nerves and is referred to the dermatomes of the same segments; reflex afferents travel with CN IX and CN X.
Carotid sinus (CN IX) and aortic arch (CN X) baroreceptors excite the nucleus solitarius, which raises vagal and lowers sympathetic output when pressure rises.

verify: Proportions of corticospinal fibers from area 4, area 6, and parietal cortex (about one third each), the Betz cell fraction (about 3%), and the fraction crossing at the decussation (75% to 90% across sources) vary; confirm the values NABNE uses.

The level of origin of the great anterior radicular artery varies widely (commonly quoted T9 to T12, range about T8 to L2, usually on the left); confirm whether NABNE expects a level or the eponym artery of Adamkiewicz.

The mechanism by which B12 deficiency damages myelin (impaired methylation through S-adenosylmethionine versus abnormal fatty acids from methylmalonyl-CoA) is not settled; the chapter states the enzyme defects without assigning cause.
ALS genetics: about 10% familial is consensus; relative frequencies of C9orf72 and SOD1 differ by population and source.
Duration of spinal shock in humans is quoted from days to several weeks, and the T6 threshold for neurogenic hypotension is approximate.
Referral segments differ slightly between Moore and other texts (heart T1 to T4 or T5, kidney and ureter T10 or T11 to L1 or L2); values here are approximate.
Carotid sinus operating range (about 50 to 60 mmHg threshold, saturation near 180 mmHg) follows Guyton and Hall; other texts give slightly different limits.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Betz cells, artery of Adamkiewicz, Argyll Robertson pupils, Charcot joints, and Werdnig-Hoffmann disease (severe infantile SMA).
